tldr: Built on the fast VIO system Basalt, RootSLAM introduces loop closure and a specialized 'square root bundle adjustment' that stably solves in single-precision floating point, achieving up to 20x faster speeds while matching or exceeding state-of-the-art accuracy.
hero_caption: Results of RootSLAM processing a long 42-minute public dataset sequence (MOO12). In the top map, a consistent long-term trajectory (gray) and landmarks (blue) are estimated. As shown in the bottom execution time graph, the system continuously runs at an average of 7.2 ms, well below the 33 ms real-time budget for 30 fps across 99.99% of frames.
overview:
For edge devices such as drones, XR headsets, and autonomous driving platforms, Visual-Inertial SLAM (VI-SLAM)—estimating pose and mapping an environment simultaneously using cameras and an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU)—is essential. Deep learning-based SLAM systems have gained attention recently, but they suffer from high computational overhead and strictly require GPUs. Meanwhile, classical geometry-based methods retain superior computational efficiency, yet face trade-offs: OKVIS2 is computationally heavy, while ORB-SLAM3 tends to lose trajectory smoothness over long-term tracking.

To address this, the authors turned to Basalt, a fast, lightweight VIO with smooth local tracking. While Basalt excels at local smoothness, it lacks loop closure (correcting drift when returning to previously visited places), leading to unbounded global drift. To solve this, the authors developed RootSLAM. It integrates a persistent map for long-term retention, an asynchronous loop detection and optimization module, and a global bundle adjustment that reformulates the Structure from Motion (SfM) square root bundle adjustment (RootBA) for VI-SLAM.

Standard optimization forms normal equations, which squares the condition number and mandates double-precision (64-bit) computation. By combining a square root formulation directly with pose-graph constraints, RootSLAM enables stable optimization in single precision (32-bit). Evaluated across 103 real-world dataset sequences, RootSLAM achieves trajectory accuracy competitive with or better than state-of-the-art methods while running up to 20 times faster.
contributions: Built a multi-camera VI-SLAM system that matches or exceeds the accuracy of state-of-the-art methods (OKVIS2 and ORB-SLAM3) while running up to 20 times faster
Integrated SfM square root bundle adjustment with pose-graph constraints, doubling optimization performance by stably solving global map optimization in single-precision (32-bit) floating point
Ensured complete geometric consistency for multi-camera setups through a rigorous camera rig formulation and support for arbitrary camera models
Open-sourced the full pipeline, including persistent map management, fast loop detection, pose-graph optimization, and global bundle adjustment

sections.heading: Why Ultra-Fast Geometry-Based VI-SLAM Is Needed Now
sections.summary: Robotics and XR devices require low-latency, low-power self-localization. Because deep learning-based approaches carry heavy compute burdens, this paper extends the highly efficient geometry-based VIO Basalt to propose RootSLAM, combining state-of-the-art accuracy with up to 20x faster speeds.
sections.details:
With the rise of spatial computing and autonomous mobile robots, real-time pose estimation on small, power-constrained devices is increasingly vital. At the core of this effort is Visual-Inertial SLAM (VI-SLAM), which combines cameras and an IMU. Multi-camera setups are especially effective for reducing depth ambiguity and widening the field of view.

Recent research in learning-based SLAM has shown state-of-the-art accuracy, but network-based geometry estimation and GPU reliance incur substantial computational overhead. Furthermore, recent insights reveal that the high accuracy of learning-based methods stems largely from improved feature tracking; integrating similar trackers into classical geometry-based pipelines often makes classical methods outperform them. Thus, for practical deployment on edge devices, classical geometry-based methods retain a major advantage.

However, existing top-tier geometry-based VI-SLAM systems like ORB-SLAM3 and OKVIS2 still suffer from long runtimes or degraded local trajectory smoothness. Therefore, the authors chose Basalt—known for its smooth tracking—as their foundation. By adapting SfM square root bundle adjustment to VI-SLAM, RootSLAM doubles optimization speed using single-precision computation and runs up to 20 times faster overall than state-of-the-art systems.

sections.heading: From Filtering to Sliding Windows, and on to Square Root Optimization
sections.summary: SLAM evolved from filtering methods like EKF to high-accuracy sliding-window nonlinear optimization. This section reviews the strengths and weaknesses of prior VI-SLAM systems and outlines the lineage of square root formulations that solve large-scale bundle adjustment in single precision.
sections.details:
The history of VIO began with extended Kalman filters (EKFs) like MSCKF and iterated EKFs (IEKFs) like ROVIO. Although lightweight with low compute requirements, they lag behind modern sliding-window nonlinear least-squares optimization (which optimizes a recent set of keyframes) in metrics like Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE).

Among optimization-based systems, OKVIS, the ORB-SLAM series, and Basalt are widely known. Basalt pairs FAST corners with KLT optical flow (local patch tracking) and smartly marginalizes old keyframes, producing exceptionally smooth trajectory estimates. However, Basalt is a pure VIO system without loop closure to correct drift upon revisiting locations, meaning global errors inevitably accumulate over long trajectories.

Conversely, OKVIS2 boasts top-tier accuracy but is computationally very heavy, while ORB-SLAM3 tends to degrade local Relative Trajectory Error (RTE, trajectory jitter) during loop corrections. In addition, global bundle adjustment (GBA) for refining the whole map suffers from squaring the Hessian condition number when forming normal equations. Consequently, double precision (64-bit float) is mandatory for numerical stability, driving up computational costs.

Addressing this issue, Demmel et al. (RootBA) proposed square root bundle adjustment, projecting out landmarks via QR decomposition to avoid forming normal equations. This demonstrated that high accuracy could be maintained in single precision (32-bit). The novelty of this work lies in extending this square root approach from SfM to multi-camera VI-SLAM and fusing it with pose-graph constraints.

sections.heading: The Three Pillars of RootSLAM and the Reformulated Square Root BA
sections.summary: On top of Basalt's VIO front end, RootSLAM adds a persistent map, asynchronous loop closing, and a newly developed global square root bundle adjustment. By integrating pose-graph constraints as Jacobian rows rather than into the Hessian, global optimization runs stably in single precision.
sections.details:
RootSLAM retains Basalt's fast front end and local optimization, connecting three new components as shown in Figure F2.

### III-A Persistent Map
Keyframes and landmarks that slide out of the local optimization window are retained in a persistent map instead of being discarded. Simultaneously, a covisibility graph tracking co-observed landmarks between keyframes is kept up to date. To prevent unbounded map growth and compute failure, redundant keyframes sharing over 90% observations with at least three other keyframes are culled. If keyframe count exceeds 1500, the 30 lowest-scoring keyframes based on quality and covisibility redundancy are automatically discarded.

### III-B Loop Detection and Closing
To avoid blocking the local tracking thread, loop processing runs completely asynchronously in a separate thread. When a keyframe is created, candidate frames are queried using the fast Bag-of-Words library HashBoW and ORB descriptors. Candidates must pass strict checks: brute-force matching, landmark reprojection, and geometric verification via the gP3P algorithm. If estimated drift is below 10 cm, overlapping landmarks are simply merged. If drift exceeds 10 cm, pose-graph optimization (PGO) is triggered to correct global map distortion. As shown in Figure F3, only the necessary detected loops are selected and forwarded to pose-graph optimization.

### III-C Global Optimization
As the final stage of the pipeline, global bundle adjustment refines the entire map. Original RootBA targeted SfM, where camera intrinsics were unknown and monocular setups were assumed. This work introduces three key adaptations:
- Omitting intrinsics: SLAM uses pre-calibrated cameras, so intrinsics should remain fixed. Removing intrinsics from the state vector reduces optimization variables from 9 to 6 degrees of freedom (rigid body transformation only) per camera.
- Optimizing camera rig poses: To enforce the rigid body constraint between cameras and the IMU body frame, the body pose $x_b$ is optimized rather than individual camera poses. Using the chain rule with adjoint representations, observations across all rig cameras are aggregated into a single landmark block.
- Adding a pose-graph regularization term: Bundle adjustment only constrains frames sharing co-observed landmarks, but odometry edges and past loop-closure edges should also be leveraged. The proposed method adds pose-graph residuals $r_{ab}$ directly as a new row block beneath the reduced camera Jacobian $Q_2^T J_p$. This preserves the square root formulation and allows stable solving in single-precision floating point (32-bit) without explicitly forming the ill-conditioned Hessian.

sections.heading: Comparison with State of the Art: Up to 20x Faster with Matching Accuracy
sections.summary: Evaluated across 103 sequences in EuRoC, TUM-VI, and MSD. Single-precision optimization provided a 2.16x speedup without accuracy loss. RootSLAM achieved equal or better trajectory accuracy than OKVIS2 and ORB-SLAM3 while delivering up to 20x faster processing speeds.
sections.details:
Evaluation was conducted on 103 sequences across the Monado SLAM Dataset (MSD), which features rapid head movements on VR headsets, and standard benchmarks EuRoC and TUM-VI. Baseline Basalt, OKVIS2, and ORB-SLAM3 served as comparison targets.

In the ablation study (Table I), adding loop closure (+LC) to Basalt reduced the Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) on the MIP group from 23.6 cm to 4.0 cm (nearly a 6x reduction), and full RootSLAM (RS) reached 2.4 cm (nearly 10x). Notably, adding only global BA (+GBA) prioritized global consistency at the cost of local smoothness (RTE). However, introducing the proposed pose-graph constraint improved ATE while restoring smoothness (RTE) to levels equal to or better than the original VIO.

In the precision analysis (Table II), the ATE difference between double precision (float64) and single precision (float32) was under 1 cm across nearly all groups, proving practically zero accuracy loss. Meanwhile, single precision accelerated global optimization by an average of 2.16x (up to 2.54x outdoors).

In state-of-the-art accuracy comparisons (Table III, Figure F5), RootSLAM secured the best ATE across all groups in the high-motion MSD dataset. On the MIO sequence, OKVIS2 scored 451.7 cm and ORB-SLAM3 failed at 398.9 m, whereas RootSLAM maintained a precise 7.0 cm. For frame tracking completion rate, ORB-SLAM3 averaged 94.1% (dropping to 87.1% on MIO) due to lost tracking, whereas RootSLAM maintained 100%.

Execution speed highlights the system's biggest advantage (Table IV, Figure F6). On the long 42-minute MOO12 sequence, the VIO pipeline averaged 7.2 ms, far below the 33 ms budget for 30 Hz. Across 12 representative sequences, mean per-frame processing time was 10.8 ms—13x faster than OKVIS2 and 3.6x faster than ORB-SLAM3. On the long TM1 sequence (772 s), OKVIS2 took 3173 s due to map bloat (over 4x slower than real time), while RootSLAM finished in 157 s including global BA (roughly 5x faster than real time), marking a 20x speedup.

captions.F5: Comparison of ground truth (dashed line) and estimated trajectories on three representative dataset segments. On the MIPP01 sequence (left), featuring fast head rotations, OKVIS2 and ORB-SLAM3 drift significantly, while RootSLAM (blue) tracks ground truth accurately.
captions.F6: Breakdown of execution times and queue sizes on the 42-minute MOO12 sequence. (a) VIO processing time for pose output consistently stays below 10 ms, (b) queue buildup remains brief, and (c) heavy pose-graph optimization (PGO: mean 150.9 ms) easily completes within the 233 ms keyframe interval.

sections.heading: Summary and the Future of Edge Perception Systems
sections.summary: RootSLAM is a complete VI-SLAM system fusing Basalt's fast local tracking with a persistent map and square root global bundle adjustment. Delivering state-of-the-art accuracy in single precision with up to a 20x speedup, it enables advanced spatial perception on small, low-power devices.
sections.details:
This work proposed RootSLAM, a new multi-camera VI-SLAM system. Built on Basalt's smooth-tracking VIO core, it integrates a persistent map with keyframe culling, HashBoW-based asynchronous loop detection, and a global optimization stage adapting SfM square root bundle adjustment to SLAM.

Its key theoretical contributions include formulating rigid body constraints for multi-camera rigs and incorporating pose-graph constraints as additional Jacobian rows. This prevents numerical ill-conditioning and allows global optimization to execute entirely in single-precision floating point (32-bit), halving compute time without sacrificing accuracy.

Across 103 diverse datasets, RootSLAM proved competitive with or superior to top VI-SLAM systems like ORB-SLAM3 and OKVIS2 in global and local accuracy, while running up to 20x faster and avoiding runtime blowups over long sequences. The implementation will be open-sourced, marking a substantial step forward for pose estimation on edge devices with severe thermal and compute constraints, such as XR glasses and micro-drones.

takeaways: Square root bundle adjustment (RootBA) is effective not just for SfM, but also for VI-SLAM global optimization when pose-graph constraints are added as Jacobian row blocks
Using QR decomposition without forming normal equations allows global optimization to solve in single precision (32-bit), cutting compute time roughly in half without accuracy loss
While global BA alone can degrade local smoothness (RTE), combining it with pose-graph regularization achieves both smooth tracking and global accuracy
Keyframe culling is vital for long-term SLAM, preventing computational divergence while maintaining real-time performance
limitations: In challenging scenarios with minimal visual overlap between start and return locations (such as the TUM-VI outdoor TO sequences), loop closure can fail, leaving several meters of drift
The persistent map uses fixed parameters, such as a 1500 keyframe ceiling and a 90% observation overlap culling threshold; dynamic scaling strategies will be required for even larger environments
